title: Lectio in the cloister
hookLine: reading slowly, chewing words like a cow chews cud

lines: IDLENESS, THE ENEMY OF THE SOUL.
cards: Idleness is the enemy of the soul. That's how Benedict opens his chapter on the daily work. But he doesn't fill every hour with labor.

He splits the day between work with the hands and holy reading. Lectio divina, he calls it. And in the long season of Lent, each monk is handed a book from the library, to read through from start to finish.
Then, the Rule says, a senior monk or two should go round the monastery during the reading hours, to make sure nobody's idling or chatting instead of reading.
Picture a quiet covered walkway, monks on benches with books open, and someone strolling past to keep them honest.

teach.b: Lectio means reading. But not the kind you do on a phone, scrolling for the next thing. Some monastic writers reached for a farmyard picture: a cow chewing the cud.
The cow eats, rests, brings it back up, and chews again, getting everything out of it. A Carthusian monk named Guigo set out four steps. Reading puts the food in your mouth.
Meditation chews it and breaks it down. Prayer tastes it.
And contemplation is the sweetness itself. The Bible already talks about words this way.

A psalm says, "How sweet are thy words unto my taste! yea, sweeter than honey to my mouth!" Ezekiel is handed a scroll and told to eat it, and he says, "Then did I eat it; and it was in my mouth as honey for sweetness."

Words you take in and digest, not just pass your eyes over. And the very first psalm describes the blessed man as the one whose "delight is in the law of the LORD; and in his law doth he meditate day and night."
Day and night is a long time to chew one thing. Lectio isn't about how much you read. It's how long you stay with a little.
One verse, turned over and over, until something in it opens. And pairing it with work does something. The chewing carries on.

teach.h: IT GOES OUT TO THE GARDEN.
teach.b: The verse from the morning reading goes out to the garden, and comes back up between rows of beans. The cloister's just where it starts.

how: Benedictine monks and nuns set aside daily time for lectio divina, slow prayerful reading of scripture, and lay Christians, Catholic and Protestant, also practice it by reading a short passage several times and staying with a word or phrase.

games.q: it's Lent. you've been handed a book from the monastery library. how does the Rule want you to read it?
o: skim the best chapters and return it.
read it through, from start to finish.
pass it on to a brother who reads faster.
games.why: each monk receives a book from the library to read through in full, and seniors go round the monastery to see it's read.

practice: Take today's psalm line, how sweet are thy words unto my taste, and say it once, slowly, under your breath.

Say it again, leaning on a different word each time, how sweet, thy words, unto my taste, and stay with whichever word catches; when your mind drifts, come back to the verse. If you'd rather choose another line you love, do.

wordCard.voice: Lectio in the cloister. Holy reading, done slowly, in the monastery's quiet walkway, words chewed and tasted rather than skimmed.

orig.note: Latin, from Rule chapter forty-eight: holy reading.

carryVoice: Your line: chew it slowly. A little, for a long time. Rest well.
